alt: Flow chart of air separation: air is filtered, carbon dioxide and water vapour are removed, the air is compressed and cooled, then expanded through a valve until it liquefies at about −200 °C, and the liquid air is fractionally distilled in a column where nitrogen (−196 °C) leaves as a gas at the top, argon (−186 °C) part-way up and oxygen (−183 °C) as a liquid at the bottom.
caption: Figure: liquefying and fractionally distilling air

alt: Displayed formulae of the first four alkanes, methane CH4, ethane C2H6, propane C3H8 and butane C4H10: every carbon atom has four single bonds, each straight-chain alkane differs from the next by one CH2 group, and the molecular formula fits CnH2n+2.
caption: Figure: methane, ethane, propane and butane; each carbon forms four single bonds

alt: Electrolysis cell for aluminium: purified aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite at about 950 degrees Celsius in a steel tank lined with carbon, which is the negative cathode; carbon anodes dip in from above; aluminium ions gain electrons to form molten aluminium that sinks to the bottom and is tapped off, oxide ions lose electrons to form oxygen which burns the carbon anodes away as carbon dioxide.
caption: Figure: the cell used to extract aluminium

alt: Atom of potassium-39: a nucleus of 19 protons and 20 neutrons (mass number 39) surrounded by 19 electrons in shells of 2, 8, 8 and 1; the numbers of protons and electrons are equal so the atom is neutral.
caption: Figure: the particles in an atom of potassium-39

alt: Blast furnace: haematite, coke and limestone are fed in at the top and hot air is blown in near the bottom; carbon burns to carbon dioxide (C + O2), carbon dioxide is reduced to carbon monoxide (C + CO2), carbon monoxide reduces iron(III) oxide to iron (Fe2O3 + 3CO), limestone decomposes and its calcium oxide reacts with silicon dioxide to make slag; molten slag floats on molten iron and both are tapped off at the bottom, while waste gases leave at the top.
caption: Figure: the blast furnace with its main reactions

alt: Apparatus for the enthalpy change of combustion: a spirit burner containing the fuel, weighed before and after, heats a copper can holding a measured mass of water, with a thermometer and stirrer in the water and a draught shield around the flame; the rise in water temperature gives q = m c ΔT.
caption: Figure: measuring the energy released when a fuel burns

alt: Paper chromatography: a pencil base line above the solvent level in a covered beaker, and a chromatogram where the solvent front is 8.0 cm above the base line; dye A has moved 3.6 cm (Rf = 0.45), dye B 5.6 cm (Rf = 0.70), and the mixture separates into both spots.
caption: Figure: set-up and chromatogram; Rf = distance moved by the spot ÷ distance moved by the solvent front

alt: Flow chart of the Contact process: sulfur is burned or sulfide ore roasted in air to make sulfur dioxide, the gases are cleaned and dried, sulfur dioxide and oxygen react over a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst at about 450 °C and 2 atm to make sulfur trioxide, which is absorbed in 98% sulfuric acid to form oleum, and water is then added to make concentrated sulfuric acid.
caption: Figure: the Contact process in three stages

alt: Dot-and-cross diagrams: ammonia NH3 has nitrogen sharing one pair with each of three hydrogen atoms, leaving one non-bonding pair; carbon dioxide has carbon sharing two pairs with each oxygen atom (two double bonds); every atom ends with a full outer shell.
caption: Figure: shared pairs in ammonia and carbon dioxide (outer shells only)

alt: Fractionating column for crude oil: hot vapour enters near the bottom and the column is cooler towards the top; from the top down the fractions drawn off are refinery gas (1 to 4 carbon atoms), gasoline, naphtha, kerosene, diesel oil, fuel oil, lubricating oil and bitumen (more than 50), so chain length and boiling point increase down the column.
caption: Figure: the fractions of crude oil, top to bottom

alt: Two schematic graphs for a reversible reaction in a closed container: on the left the reactant concentration falls and the product concentration rises until both become constant (not equal) at equilibrium; on the right the forward rate falls and the reverse rate rises until they are equal at the same moment.
caption: Figure: at equilibrium the concentrations stop changing because the forward and reverse rates are equal

alt: Hofmann voltameter electrolysing acidified water: hydrogen collects at the negative electrode and oxygen at the positive electrode, and the volume of hydrogen, 40.0 cm3, is twice the volume of oxygen, 20.0 cm3, which shows the formula of water is H2O.
caption: Figure: a Hofmann voltameter; the gas volumes are read from the scale beside each tube

alt: Electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide: graphite electrodes dip into the melt, connected through a bulb to a d.c. supply; positive lead ions move to the negative cathode and form molten lead, negative bromide ions move to the positive anode and form brown bromine vapour.
caption: Figure: an electrolytic cell for molten lead(II) bromide

alt: Shell diagrams: lithium 2,1 has two occupied shells and one outer electron; aluminium 2,8,3 has three shells and three outer electrons; chlorine 2,8,7 has three shells and seven outer electrons. The number of shells gives the period and the outer electrons give the group.
caption: Figure: electrons in shells for lithium (2,1), aluminium (2,8,3) and chlorine (2,8,7)

alt: Cell for copper-plating an iron key: the key is connected to the negative terminal and is the cathode, a strip of copper joined to the positive terminal is the anode, and the electrolyte is copper(II) sulfate solution; copper ions gain electrons and coat the key while the copper anode dissolves to replace them.
caption: Figure: the object to be plated is the cathode and the anode is the plating metal

alt: Reaction pathway diagram with and without a catalyst: the reactants are at 0 and the products at −40 kJ/mol in both cases, so ΔH = −40 is unchanged, but the catalysed pathway (dashed) peaks at +110 kJ/mol instead of +180 kJ/mol, so the activation energy is 70 kJ/mol lower.
caption: Figure: a catalyst lowers the peak (Ea) but leaves the reactant and product levels, and so ΔH, unchanged

alt: Two reaction pathway diagrams with energies relative to the reactants: reaction A is exothermic, the products lie 45 kJ/mol below the reactants (ΔH = −45) and the peak is 120 kJ/mol above the reactants (Ea = 120); reaction B is endothermic, the products lie 65 kJ/mol above the reactants (ΔH = +65) and the peak is 210 kJ/mol above (Ea = 210).
caption: Figure: Ea is measured from the reactants to the peak; ΔH is measured from the reactants to the products

alt: Fractional distillation apparatus: a flask of ethanol and water is heated below a fractionating column packed with glass beads; the thermometer at the top reads 78 degrees Celsius while ethanol, the lower-boiling liquid, reaches the top first, passes into the Liebig condenser and is collected, while water (100 degrees Celsius) condenses in the column and runs back.
caption: Figure: fractional distillation of ethanol and water

alt: Three ways of collecting a gas: over water in an upturned jar for gases that are insoluble in water such as hydrogen and oxygen; by downward delivery into an upright jar for gases denser than air such as carbon dioxide, chlorine and sulfur dioxide; and by upward delivery into an upturned jar for gases less dense than air such as hydrogen and ammonia.
caption: Figure: choosing how to collect a gas

alt: Giant covalent structures: in diamond each carbon atom bonds to four others in a rigid three-dimensional network; in graphite each carbon bonds to three others in flat hexagonal layers, with only weak forces between the layers so they slide over each other.
caption: Figure: the structures of diamond and graphite

alt: Flow chart of the Haber process: nitrogen from air and hydrogen from methane and steam are mixed 1 to 3 by volume and compressed to about 200 atm, pass over an iron catalyst at about 450 °C in the converter where about 15% becomes ammonia, are cooled so that ammonia liquefies and is run off, and the unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled back to the compressor.
caption: Figure: the Haber process; unreacted gases are recycled

alt: Heating curve of water from ice at −20 °C to steam: temperature rises from A to B, stays flat at 0 °C from B to C while ice melts, rises from C to D (0 to 100 °C), stays flat at 100 °C from D to E while water boils (a longer flat section than melting), then steam warms from E to F.
caption: Figure: heating curve of water; the flat sections are the changes of state

alt: Dot-and-cross diagrams: sodium transfers its one outer electron to chlorine, giving Na+ (outer shell of 8 crosses) and Cl- (8 outer electrons, 7 dots and 1 cross), formula NaCl; magnesium transfers two electrons to oxygen, giving Mg2+ and O2- each with a full outer shell, formula MgO.
caption: Figure: electron transfer in sodium chloride and magnesium oxide

alt: A slice through a sodium chloride lattice: smaller positive sodium ions and larger negative chloride ions alternate in rows and columns, each ion surrounded by ions of opposite charge, in the ratio 1 to 1.
caption: Figure: a layer of the giant ionic lattice of sodium chloride

alt: Displayed formulae of the two isomers of C4H10: butane, a straight chain of four carbon atoms with a boiling point of −1 °C, and methylpropane, a chain of three carbon atoms with a CH3 branch on the middle carbon and a boiling point of −12 °C; the same molecular formula but different structural formulae.
caption: Figure: structural isomers of C₄H₁₀

alt: Apparatus for measuring the volume of gas: magnesium and dilute hydrochloric acid in a conical flask closed with a bung, a delivery tube leading to a gas syringe whose plunger moves out as hydrogen collects, with the volume read at regular times.
caption: Figure: following a reaction by collecting the gas in a gas syringe

alt: Volume of hydrogen against time from the worked example: 0, 20, 36, 48, 56, 60, 62, 62 cm³ at 10 s intervals; the curve is steepest at the start (average rate 1.8 cm³/s over the first 20 s), the gradient falls as the acid is used up and the curve is flat at 62 cm³ from 60 s when the reaction has finished.
caption: Figure: the rate graph from Example 1; the dashed line shows the average rate over the first 20 s

alt: Metallic bonding: a regular lattice of positive metal ions surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons that are free to move; when a force is applied, layers of ions slide over each other while the electrons still hold the structure together, so the metal bends instead of shattering.
caption: Figure: positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons, and layers sliding

alt: Volume of gas against time from the lesson's magnesium and acid experiment: crosses at 0, 28, 48, 62, 70, 72 and 72 cm³ every 20 s with a smooth curve of best fit through them, steepest at the start (28 cm³ in the first 20 s, 1.4 cm³/s) and level at 72 cm³ from 100 s when the magnesium is used up.
caption: Figure: points plotted as crosses with one smooth curve of best fit

alt: Graph of mass of carbon dioxide lost against time for 5 g of marble: the powder curve is steeper and levels off sooner than the chips curve, but both level off at the same 2.2 g because the same amount of calcium carbonate is used and the acid is in excess.
caption: Figure: powder reacts faster (steeper curve) but gives the same total CO₂

alt: Graph of volume of hydrogen against time for two experiments with 1.3 g of zinc and excess acid: curve B (zinc powder) is steeper at the start and levels off sooner than curve A (zinc granules), but both level off at the same final volume, 480 cm³.
caption: Figure: A is zinc granules and B is zinc powder

alt: Two scale readings worked out in the lesson: a thermometer with one small division equal to 1 degree Celsius whose liquid stops halfway between the third and fourth marks above 20 degrees, reading 23.5 degrees Celsius; and a measuring cylinder with five small divisions between each 10 cm3 mark, so one division is 2 cm3, with the bottom of the meniscus on the second small mark above 70, reading 74 cm3.
caption: Figure: find the value of one division first, then count up from the last numbered mark

alt: Filtration apparatus: a mixture of sand and salt solution is poured into a filter paper cone in a funnel; the insoluble sand stays on the paper as the residue and the salt solution runs through into the conical flask as the filtrate.
caption: Figure: filtration separates an insoluble solid (residue) from a liquid (filtrate)

alt: Simple distillation apparatus: salt solution is heated in a flask with a thermometer bulb level with the side arm; steam passes into a Liebig condenser with cold water entering at the bottom and leaving at the top, and pure water (distillate) drips into a beaker while the salt stays in the flask.
caption: Figure: simple distillation separates a solvent from a solution

alt: A simple cell: a zinc strip and a copper strip in dilute sulfuric acid joined through a voltmeter; zinc, the more reactive metal, loses electrons and dissolves, so it is the negative electrode, the electrons flow through the wire from zinc to copper, and hydrogen ions gain electrons at the copper, which is the positive electrode, forming hydrogen bubbles.
caption: Figure: a zinc–copper cell; electrons flow through the wire from the more reactive metal

alt: Solubility curve of potassium nitrate: solubility rises from 13.3 g per 100 g of water at 0 degrees Celsius to 31.6 g at 20 degrees and 110 g at 60 degrees, so cooling a saturated solution from 60 to 20 degrees crystallises 78.4 g per 100 g of water.
caption: Figure: solubility of potassium nitrate in water against temperature

alt: Flow chart for making a soluble salt from an acid and an excess of an insoluble solid: warm the dilute acid, add the solid until some is left over, filter off the excess, heat the filtrate until crystals form on a cold glass rod, cool so crystals form, then filter, wash with a little cold distilled water and dry the crystals.
caption: Figure: Method A, acid plus excess insoluble solid

alt: Particle diagrams of the three states: in a solid the particles are in a regular pattern and touching; in a liquid they are close together in an irregular arrangement; in a gas they are far apart and move randomly and quickly in all directions.
caption: Figure: the arrangement of particles in a solid, a liquid and a gas

alt: Titration set-up: acid in a burette with a tap above a conical flask holding 25.0 cm3 of alkali and a few drops of indicator, standing on a white tile so the end-point colour change is easy to see.
caption: Figure: titration apparatus

alt: The pH scale from 0 to 14 with universal indicator colours: red for pH 0 to 2 (strongly acidic), orange for 3 and 4, yellow for 5 and 6, green at pH 7 (neutral), blue for 8 to 10, and purple for 11 to 14 (strongly alkaline).
caption: Figure: universal indicator colours on the pH scale (the colour is also named above each group)
